newsitem.title: USA: Dlr extends overseas losses, ends weaker in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Dlr extends overseas losses, ends weaker in U.S.

text.p: The dollar ended modestly weaker against the mark and extended sharp overseas losses versus the yen in cross-driven U.S. trade on Thursday.

Yen buying emerged in Asian trade and continued in the U.S. after the release of strong Japanese industrial production data. Lingering talk that Japanese multinationals would convert their foreign exchange holdings into yen ahead of the March 31 fiscal year-end also helped the yen.
The retreat pushed the dollar back to its lowest intraday level against the yen in a month.

After rising by roughly nine yen -- over seven percent -- in the first six weeks of the year to reach a four-year peak of 124.82 on February 14, the dollar has dropped by over four yen in the past two weeks.

"The fear of yen repatriation and the sense that the Japanese economy may do better makes the dollar and yen a much more difficult pick," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
"The market just doesn't seem to have the willingness at this point to take the dollar any higher against the yen," he added.

The dollar ended the day at 120.60/70 yen, down from 121.02/07 yen at the open and 122.16/26 at Wednesday's close. Against the mark, the dollar ended modestly lower at 1.6875/80 against 1.6897/02 at the open.

In a rare sign of Japanese economic strength, industrial production for January rose a preliminary 5.3 percent from December, up sharply from a modest 0.1 percent rise in the previous month and higher than most economists' expectations.
Currency traders said the data contributed to the view that the Japanese economy may be on the road to recovery, fueling purchases of yen against the dollar.

Also boosting the Japanese currency and weighing on the dollar was lingering talk that Japanese multinational corporations will repatriate their currency holdings into yen ahead of Japan's fiscal year-end.

Though no concrete signs of such repatriation have emerged since Mitsubishi Heavy Industries announced on Monday that it planned to convert $700 million in foreign currency deposits into yen by the end of March, traders said the yen would continue to benefit from the talk in the weeks ahead.

"The fact is that between now and the end of March you are going to continue to see the yen strengthen because of the possibility of repatriation and because of some actual repatriation," said Richard Vullo, vice president at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank in New York.
Against the mark, the dollar was only modestly weaker, retreating briefly after the Dutch central bank hiked its key special advances interest rate to 2.70 percent from 2.50 percent.

The mark touched a nine month low against the yen at 71.41 on Thursday, and traders said this weakness kept the dollar's losses against the German currency in check, even as it hurt the dollar against the yen.
In other trade, the dollar retreated to close at 1.4730/40 Swiss francs against 1.4758/63 at the open, after the Swiss National Bank left interest rates unchanged.

The British pound dropped slightly to $1.6265/70 against $1.6270/75 in early trade, while the dollar ended at Canadian $1.3675/80, modestly up from C$1.3667/72. The Australian dollar settled at $0.7752/57 versus $0.7787/92 at the open.
